To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) BIs have evolved over the past 40 years; 2) older BIs are not adapting to new paradigms; 3) tenants in older generation incubators make less use of BI services than tenants in younger generation incubators; and 4) this is a consequence, at least in part, of slack selection criteria, the absence of exit policies, and the lack of a clear value proposition.

(i) the service provision and the selection criteria in business incubators have evolved over the years, (ii) the service portfolio of the older generations of incubators is more diverse than that of the newer ones, and (iii) the tenants of older generation incubators are less satisfied with the services provided by their incubator than tenants in younger generation incubators.
older generation BUs are less effective than newer generation incubators.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the business incubation industry has evolved over the years.
understanding the evolution of business incubators and the extent to which the services they offer have adapted to meet tenants’ needs.
the question of how the provision of business incubation has changed in the past decade, and how this change is related to the evolution of incubation paradigmas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
business incubators are not just a one-size-fits-all solution to economic development.
the evolution of business incubators has not been linear and that the evolution of BIs has been driven more by the demand of the tenants than by the supply of the incubators themselves.
the evolution of incubation is still ongoing and it is not yet clear what the next generation of incubation will be like.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
business incubators should be aware of the evolution in the demand for business incubation services and should be able to adjust their value proposition accordingly.

business incubators are still relevant and that there is a demand for incubation services, but that the services provided need to be more focused on the needs of the tenants and that the selection criteria should be stricter to avoid tenants that will not benefit from incubation.
business incubators have to be flexible in order to meet the needs of their tenants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of BIs should not be considered as a simple linear progression from one generation to the next.
the value proposition of BIs needs to be updated to incorporate recent incubator paradigms, which is a challenge for BIs’ management, prospective tenants and policymakers alike.
business incubators (BIS) should update their service portfolios and introduce stricter selection criteria and exit policies.
